children: Elon Musk-led Starlink says it has established dedicated infrastructure and secured requisite government approvals, as the satellite internet market awaits spectrum assignment and other operational clearances

Starlink on Friday said it was ready to provide high-speed internet services in India, claiming it had established dedicated infrastructure and secured the requisite government approvals. The statement came in response to Reliance Industries’ position that all satellite communications operators, including Starlink, must comply with Indian laws and policies.

The Elon Musk-led company made the statement on X while responding to a post by Reliance, which had said on Thursday that it welcomed competition in satellite communications but expected every operator to follow the country’s regulatory framework.

“We have worked closely with regulators, industry and operators in India for 5+ years, and built a network of dedicated systems, gateways, and other infrastructure all in-country to exclusively serve Indian traffic safely and securely — and all with the requisite government approvals. Starlink is ready to connect India with high-speed internet,” the company said.

The exchange follows a public dispute over competition and regulatory approvals in India’s satellite communications market. Musk had criticised the competitive environment, while Reliance maintained that domestic and foreign companies must operate under the same legal framework.
Reliance’s Position

In its Thursday statement, Reliance said it had never feared competition and viewed it as a test of which company served customers best. It cited the growth of its telecommunications business, Jio, since entering India’s mobile services market in 2016.
“At Reliance, we have never feared competition. We see it as the truest test of who serves the customer best,” the company said.
Reliance said Jio had built a customer base of more than 530 million over the past decade, offering affordable data services and digital infrastructure.
“We welcome competition in satellite communications, including Starlink. Every player, Jio included, must serve the people of India and abide by the laws and policies of the land,” it said.
The company also said India’s openness to investment and innovation depended on adherence to the rule of law. It noted that Jio’s own satellite services were awaiting clearances.

The statement followed Musk’s criticism of India’s satellite communications market. In posts on X, he accused powerful business interests of seeking to preserve a “monopolistic chokehold” on Indian consumers and sarcastically referred to Reliance Industries Chairman Mukesh Ambani as “Prime Minister Ambani”, questioning his influence over government decisions.

The Ministry of Communications rejected allegations that India’s regulatory framework was unfair or discriminatory, describing such suggestions as “baseless and misconceived”. Government sources have said companies must comply with Indian laws to operate in the country.
Licences And Approvals

Starlink, Reliance’s Jio Satcom and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb are pursuing opportunities in India’s satellite communications market. Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia has said the three ventures have secured satellite communications licences, while Amazon’s Project Kuiper has also expressed interest in the market.
However, a licence alone does not permit commercial operations. Satellite operators must meet security requirements and obtain spectrum assignment under the applicable regulatory framework.

Scindia has said spectrum will be assigned after the government finalises a revenue-based charging framework and individual operators fulfil the required security conditions. The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India and the Department of Telecommunications have been working towards a decision on satellite spectrum pricing.
The distinction between licensing and operational approval remains central to the dispute, with operators awaiting the clearances needed to launch commercial services.
OneWeb Awaits Clearance
The debate has also involved Bharti Airtel Chairman Sunil Mittal, whose satellite communications venture, Eutelsat OneWeb, is awaiting permission to begin commercial operations in India.
Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026, Mittal said OneWeb was ahead of Starlink in the queue for launching services in the country.
“I think I am significantly ahead in the queue from him. I applied five years back,” Mittal said. “We don’t have the permission, so we’ll be very happy to get it at least a few days before him.”

Mittal said OneWeb’s ground network had been ready for three years and its satellites had been hovering over India for five years, but the company was still awaiting permission to begin commercial operations.
Jio’s Satellite Plans

Reliance is also pursuing its satellite communications plans, including a proposed constellation of about 1,600 low-Earth-orbit satellites intended to extend internet connectivity to 600,000 villages.
The initiative could bring Jio into more direct competition with Starlink in remote areas and locations with limited terrestrial broadband coverage.

The two companies signed an agreement last year to explore ways of bringing Starlink services to Indian customers through Jio’s retail network. The arrangement adds another dimension to their evolving relationship as both companies pursue opportunities in India’s satellite internet market.
The timing of commercial launches will depend on the applicable spectrum framework, security requirements and other regulatory conditions.
